justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline across all three horizons, starting near 155.2 for the one-day forecast and edging up to 156.5 over the one-month horizon. The one-day estimate is anchored heavily by recent price action, momentum, and mean-reversion tendencies that dominate at short horizons — essentially assuming continuity with the prevailing trend unless there is a clear catalyst to suggest otherwise. The one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a slight positive drift, consistent with a long-run expected return assumption applied to whatever underlying asset this represents, while also acknowledging that prices tend to revert to a slowly rising fundamental or trend value over medium horizons. The incremental increases in the point estimate are intentionally modest, reflecting the limited predictability of asset prices beyond very short windows.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is the expected behavior under most asset pricing models where uncertainty compounds over time. For the one-day horizon, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.4 units, reflecting typical intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, this expands to about 12.6 units, incorporating the possibility of multi-day trending moves, news events, or technical breakouts. At the one-month horizon, the interval stretches to 27 units, acknowledging that a full month allows for macroeconomic data releases, earnings, central bank decisions, and shifts in market sentiment — all of which can cumulatively push prices well away from any starting point estimate.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as an unexpected inflation print, a central bank policy surprise, or a geopolitical escalation that triggers broad risk-off or risk-on moves. A sharp liquidity event, flash crash, or short squeeze could violate the one-day interval in particular, since such events are by definition hard to anticipate and can move prices well beyond normal volatility bands in hours. On the upside, a positive earnings surprise, a regulatory catalyst, or a broader sector rotation could drive the price meaningfully above the upper bound of even the one-month interval. These tail risks are real but deliberately not fully captured in the stated intervals, as doing so would require intervals so wide they would offer little practical informational value.
